content: Unsafe abortions can lead to significant health complications, including acute care costs, long-term issues such as pelvic inflammatory disease, damage to reproductive organs, and secondary infertility. Administering antibiotic prophylaxis at the time of the procedure may help prevent these adverse outcomes if proven effective. The routine use of antibiotics before surgical evacuation of the uterus in cases of incomplete abortion remains a topic of debate. Some healthcare facilities recommend antibiotic prophylaxis as a standard practice, while others only prescribe antibiotics when there are clinical signs of infection. This review aimed to assess the effectiveness of routine antibiotic prophylaxis in women with incomplete abortion. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of databases, including the Cochrane Controlled Trials Register, PubMed/MEDLINE, EMBASE, and Popline, with the last search performed in January 2007. Randomized trials comparing routine antibiotic prophylaxis with no prophylaxis were considered for inclusion in the review. Data extraction was performed independently by two reviewers, and the quality of the included trials was assessed. Only one study, involving 140 women, met the inclusion criteria. Another well-conducted trial was excluded due to a high rate of participant loss during follow-up. The included study found no significant differences in post-abortion infection rates between the routine prophylaxis group and the control group. However, adherence to antibiotic treatment was notably low. The authors concluded that there is insufficient evidence to support or refute the routine use of antibiotic prophylaxis in women undergoing surgical management for incomplete abortion.
